## Hypothesis Testing {#slide-12}

## What are statistical hypotheses? {#slide-13}

Claims/assertions about population parameters

Tested using a single sample from the population

Any test involves two hypotheses

	The null hypothesis, H 0

	The alternative hypothesis, H a

## The Two Hypotheses {#slide-14}

The  Null Hypothesis , H 0  

Statement of 

No change

No effect

No difference

Assumed true until evidence indicates otherwise.

 The  Alternative Hypothesis,  H a

Case:   Hazelwood School District vs. United States  (1977)

Subject: 

Discrimination against African Americans in hiring school teachers.

Facts:  

In 1972 and 1973,  only 22 out of 405 (5.4%)  teachers hired were African American in Saint Louis.

All of America:  15.4% of teachers are African American

- Reject H 0    Evidence supports H a

"There is significant evidence to support..." then the alternative hypothesis statement

## Writing Conclusions: Large p-value (\> 0.05) {#slide-24}

## Hazelwood example {#slide-25}

- p-value \< 0.05    Reject H 0

There is significant evidence that the proportion of African-American teachers hired by the Saint Louis school district was less than the national rate of hire.

## Note! {#slide-26}

No conclusion EVER involves "accepting" or "supporting" H 0 !

## What if... {#slide-27}

...the sample had 52/405 African Americans?

![](ppt/media/image18.png "Picture 7")

## Which of these conclusions is best, if 52/405 were African-American? {#slide-28}

There is significant evidence that the proportion of African-American teachers hired by the Saint Louis school district was less than the national rate of hire.

There is no significant evidence that the proportion of African-American teachers hired by the Saint Louis school district was less than the national rate of hire.

There is significant evidence that the proportion of African-American teachers hired by the Saint Louis school district was equal to the national rate of hire.

Suppose that a pharmaceutical company wants to be able to claim that for its newest medication, the proportion of patients who experience side effects is less than 0.20.  In a clinical trial with 400 patients, they find that 68 of the patients experience side effects (68/400 = 17%).  Perform a hypothesis test at a 5% level of significance.

There is significant evidence that the percent of people experiencing side effects with the new drug is equal to 20%

## Moral 2 {#slide-67}

Decreasing significance level decreases power

(in general, harder to reject H 0 , when false  or  true)

Increasing significance level increases power 

(in general, easier to reject H 0 , when false  or  true)

## Example 8 {#slide-74}

Average body temperature is 'well-known' to be 98.6 o F.

A sample of 65 young healthy males resulted in a sample mean of 98.39 and standard deviation of 0.74.

Does this sample provide statistically significant evidence that the population mean body temperature of young healthy males is LOWER than 98.6 o ?

## Step 0: Parameter of interest {#slide-75}

## Step 1: Hypotheses (in general) {#slide-76}

In general, take the form:

Which H a  depends on research question.

## Step 1: Hypotheses (our example) {#slide-77}

Our example: Does this sample provide statistically significant evidence that the population mean body temperature of young healthy males is  lower  than 98.6 o ?

## Step 2: Sample result {#slide-78}

## Step 3: Find statistic, determine its distribution under H 0 {#slide-79}

## Write conclusion {#slide-82}

We have statistically significant evidence to support the alternative hypothesis, that the average body temperature of healthy young adult males is lower than 98.6 degrees F.

## Accompanying confidence interval {#slide-83}

## 95% CI interpretation {#slide-84}

We are 95% confident the true average body temperature of healthy young adult males is between 98.21 and 98.57 degrees F.

Since 95% CI does not overlap null mean of 98.6, we could use this confidence interval (instead of a test statistic/p-value) to support H a .

## Example 9  {#slide-89}

According to the United States Mint, quarters weigh 5.67 grams.  A researcher is interested in determining whether the "state" quarters have a weight that is different from 5.67 grams.  He randomly selects 18 "state" quarters, weighs them and obtains a sample mean of 5.70 and standard deviation of 0.05. Assume the distribution is normally distributed.

	

At the  α  =   0.05 level of significance, is there evidence to conclude that state quarters have a weight different than  5.67 grams (either way)? 

Follow the steps in a hypothesis test using ALL possible methods to determine significance (p-value, standardized statistic, and confidence interval).

## Example 10 {#slide-99}

A 2014 article randomized 47 children aged 6-10 to one of two groups 

( K. nan der Horst, A.  Ferrage , A.  Rytz  (2014). \"Involving Children in Meal Preparation,\" Appetite. Vol. 79, pp.18-24)

Group 1: Children helped parents with meal preparation

Group 2: Children did not help with meal preparation

Of interest: Are average number of calories consumed higher for children in the "helped" group?

![Image result for involving children in meal prep](ppt/media/image70.jpeg "Picture 5")

## Of note {#slide-100}

Groups are independent:

Randomly assigned

Number of calories consumed by a kid in the 'helped' group provides no information about number of calories consumed by a kid in the 'did not help' group

## Of note (Example 10) {#slide-101}

## Data summary {#slide-102}

There were 25 kids assigned to help with a sample mean of 431.4 and standard deviation of 105.7.

There were 22 kids assigned not to help with a sample mean of 346.8 and a standard deviation of 99.5.

## Conclusion {#slide-108}

Since the p-value \< 0.05, we have significant evidence that children who help with meal preparation consume more calories  on average  than children who do not.

Furthermore, we can be 95% confident that children who help with meal preparation consume between 24 and 144 more calories,  on average , than children who do not.
